design_detail: Secondary analysis of the two waves of NESARC, a US nationally representative household survey (Wave 1 2001–2002, n=43,093; Wave 2 2004–2005, n=34,653 re-interviewed). Past-12-month DSM-IV alcohol dependence (AD; AUDADIS-IV) at Wave 2 was split by Wave 1 status into new onset (no lifetime AD at Wave 1), persistence (past-12-month AD at Wave 1) and recurrence (lifetime but not past-12-month AD at Wave 1). The share of each in Wave 2 prevalence, and the rate of each among the people at risk, were estimated by age group (seven groups) with weighted logistic regressions adjusted for sex and race. A second set of weighted logistic regressions related three life transitions between the waves (becoming a parent, change in marital status, change in employment) to each transition, with two- and three-way interactions with age (21–37 vs 38+) and sex.
can_establish: How past-year alcohol dependence among US adults in 2001–2005 was made up of new, persistent and recurrent cases at each age, how often each transition happened over about three years among the people at risk, and whether life transitions between the interviews went with these transitions after adjustment for sex, race and age group.
cannot_establish: Whether life transitions cause changes in alcohol dependence (they were measured over the same interval as the outcome, people select into roles, and few confounders were adjusted); whether the age gradient reflects ageing rather than birth cohort (different age groups were followed over one three-year window); what happened to people who died or were not re-interviewed; whether 'offset' means lasting recovery (anyone below the full three-criterion threshold in the year before Wave 2 counted as offset); or what part treatment played (treatment between the waves is not reported).

sample.recruitment: General population, not a treatment sample: NESARC, funded by NIAAA and conducted by the US Census Bureau, a weighted representative sample of US civilians aged 18 and over, with Black and Hispanic people and young adults aged 18–24 oversampled; face-to-face interviews at both waves (Method › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All Wave 2 respondents enter the age decomposition: the six groups of Table 2 sum to 34,653 (editors' arithmetic), so the population at risk of new onset includes people who had never drunk alcohol. The life-transition models drop people with missing transition data (Table 3, note; footnote 5) and use two age groups, 21–37 and 38+ (Results › Role Transitions…, 3rd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Wave 2 (weighted): mean age 48 (SE 0.17); 52% women; 71% White non-Hispanic, 11% African American, 12% Hispanic, 4% Asian, 2% American Indian (Method › Participants). The groups with past or present AD were 65–72% men against 44.7% in the consistent non-diagnosis group, and their mean age at Wave 1 ranged from 30.4 (offset) to 41.8 (non-recurrent) against 46.4 in the consistent non-diagnosis group (Table 2).
sample.attrition: 34,653 of 43,093 Wave 1 respondents were re-interviewed (80.4%, editors' arithmetic; approximately 80% according to the Limitations). Retention was higher in women (82.7% vs 80.2% in men), at ages 30–59 than at 18–20 (79.0%), and in people with prior-to-past-year AD (85.6% vs 81.2% with no diagnosis); it was lower in Black (79.2%), Asian (73.3%) and Hispanic (73.4%) than in White respondents (83.6%), and among age groups lowest at 21–24 (76.4%) and 60 and over (76.9%) (Table 1). Wave 2 weights adjust for attrition and Wave 1 lifetime psychiatric disorders, and all analyses were repeated with multiple imputation (Method › Analysis; Results, 1st paragraph). The life-transition models lost a further 10–15% of each at-risk group to missing transition data (Table 3 against Table 2, editors' arithmetic).
sample.selection_effects: A general-population household sample re-interviewed after about three years. Age comparisons are between birth cohorts followed over the same three-year window, so age is confounded with cohort and period, which the authors set aside explicitly together with differential mortality (Introduction › The Relative Importance of Onset, Recurrence, and Persistence on Maturing Out, 1st paragraph). People who died between the waves are not in the Wave 2 sample; if mortality is higher among people with persistent AD, persistent cases would be lost preferentially at older ages (editors' inference; the paper does not examine it). The at-risk groups are defined from lifetime histories recalled at Wave 1, so forgotten earlier episodes move people from 'recurrence' into 'new onset'.

exposure.measurement: Age group: Wave 1 age plus three years, an approximation of age at Wave 2 because the interval between interviews varied; seven groups for the decomposition (the text names 21–23, 24–27, 28–32, 43–52 and 63+; the full set is printed only in the figures) and two groups (21–37, 38+) for the life-transition models. Life transitions between the waves, by self-report: becoming a parent (any own, adopted, foster or step children since the last interview); change in marital status (became married, including starting to live with someone as if married; stable; separated, divorced or widowed); change in employment (unemployed or retired at Wave 1 and employed at Wave 2; employed at Wave 1 and unemployed or retired at Wave 2; stable), coded from the two waves (Method › Measures › Life Transitions; footnotes 2–4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to the exposures. Alcohol consumption and heavy drinking were not analysed (Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph); age at first drinking ('not counting small tastes or sips') was used only to describe the groups (Method › Measures › Other variables).
exposure.polysubstance: Not measured or adjusted in this analysis: no variable for tobacco, other drug use or drug use disorders enters any model.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (household survey of alcohol-dependence status).

comparison.controls: For each transition, the people at risk who did not make it: offset (past-12-month AD at Wave 1, none at Wave 2) against persistence; non-recurrence (lifetime but not past-12-month AD at Wave 1, none at Wave 2) against recurrence; consistent non-diagnosis (no lifetime AD at Wave 1, none at Wave 2) against new onset (Results › Role Transitions and Stability and Change of AD across Development, 1st paragraph). For the life transitions the references were not becoming a parent, stable marital status (married, single or divorced at both waves) and stable employment (employed or unemployed at both waves).
comparison.matching: None. The age-group models adjust for sex and race (White against all other groups); the life-transition models contain sex, race, age group, the three transitions, and their two- and three-way interactions with age and sex (Table 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Traits related to negative emotionality and impulsivity (named by the authors as unavailable in the data set), drinking level and heavy drinking, family history of alcohol problems, other psychiatric and substance use disorders, education and income, treatment for alcohol problems between the waves, and the timing of each transition within the interval.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS-IV, the NESARC interview, scoring DSM-IV alcohol dependence (at least 3 of 7 criteria) for the past 12 months and for the period before it; prior-to-past-year dependence required the criteria to cluster within the same year (Method › Measures › Alcohol Dependence, 1st paragraph). Reliability is supported by citation (Grant et al., 1995; Grant et al., 2003).
outcomes.validity_norms: Reliability is cited, not re-examined here. The authors note that lifetime diagnoses have poor test–retest reliability (Discussion › Rethinking…, 2nd paragraph), and lifetime status at Wave 1 is what separates new onset from recurrence.
outcomes.operationalization: New onset: past-12-month AD at Wave 2 with no lifetime AD at Wave 1. Persistence: past-12-month AD at both waves; this includes episodic courses with a remission between the interviews that did not reach the year before Wave 2. Recurrence: past-12-month AD at Wave 2 after lifetime but not past-12-month AD at Wave 1. Offset, the complement of persistence and the closest this paper comes to 'maturing out' or remission: past-12-month AD at Wave 1 and not meeting full criteria in the 12 months before Wave 2, about three years later, which can include people with one or two remaining symptoms. Rates were computed among the people at risk and shares as fractions of all Wave 2 cases (Method › Measures › Alcohol Dependence, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). Whether anyone had treatment is not reported. Sensitivity analyses redefined persistence as AD at Wave 1 plus at least one dependence symptom at Wave 2, or as continuous diagnosis across the interval, and recurrence as no dependence symptom in the year before Wave 1 (Results › Alternative Definitions of Persistence and Recurrence).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three transition outcomes, each tested across seven age groups (three Wald tests) and in a life-transition model of 22 odds ratios (66 in Table 3), plus sensitivity analyses, all judged at p<0.05 without correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: face-to-face survey interviews with the AUDADIS-IV for the US Census Bureau; whether Wave 2 interviewers knew Wave 1 answers is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Shares of Wave 2 past-12-month AD (Figure 1, given in the text only for the youngest and oldest groups): persistence 29% at ages 21–23 and 27% at 63+; new onset 66% and 58%; recurrence 5% and 15%. Rates among the people at risk (Figure 2), age-group differences adjusted for sex and race: new onset Wald F=44.22, 6 df, p<.0001, and recurrence Wald F=6.64, 6 df, p<.0001, both falling with age; persistence Wald F=2.28, 6 df, p=.047, rising with age, not significant with multiple imputation. Persistence over the interval: 32.4% at ages 21–23 and 44.5% at 43–52 (Discussion); the other age-specific rates and all prevalences are printed only in Figures 1 and 2 (images, not extracted). Editors' calculation from the unweighted counts of Table 2, all ages: 422 of 1,172 people with past-12-month AD at Wave 1 (36%) met criteria again at Wave 2, so about 64% showed offset; 767 of 30,696 without lifetime AD (2.5%) had a new onset; 244 of 2,785 with earlier AD (8.8%) had a recurrence. Life-transition models (Table 3; odds ratios with 95% CIs; because the interactions are in the model, each main effect is the odds ratio in the reference groups, women aged 21–37): new onset, becoming a parent 0.39 (0.18–0.83), new job 2.79 (1.19–6.55), men vs women 1.87 (1.29–2.73), age 38+ vs 21–37 0.22 (0.14–0.34); persistence, becoming a parent 0.22 (0.06–0.82), sex × parenthood 4.56 (1.09–19.08), age × parenthood 9.56 (1.14–79.78), sex × age × parenthood 0.02 (0.00–0.28), sex × age × new job 0.03 (0.00–0.48); recurrence, no term significant (age 38+ 0.47, 0.22–1.01). Change in marital status was not significant in any model.
analysis.covariates: Age-group models: sex and race. Life-transition models: sex, race, age group, the three transitions and their interactions with age and sex. Not adjusted: drinking level, other substance use, psychiatric comorbidity, education, income, family history, treatment.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Secondary analysis of survey data; no protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 3 prints every term of the three models, and three alternative definitions are reported with their effect on the results. But several analyses are 'not shown' (the replication of Grant's 1997 persistence definition with Wave 1 data; the marital-status analysis in the whole sample), imputation results are mentioned only where they differ, and the age-specific prevalences and rates are printed only in figure images.
analysis.power: Not addressed formally. The authors state that subsamples become small when baseline diagnosis, age, sex and transition are crossed, and that they collapsed age into two groups and merged 'stable' categories for this reason (Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph); the widest intervals in Table 3 (0.00–0.28; 1.14–79.78; 0.42–83.46; 0.55–204.78) show sparse cells.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In a US general-population sample followed for about three years, the lower prevalence of past-year alcohol dependence at older ages went with steeply falling rates of new onset and of recurrence, while the persistent share of cases stayed near 27–29% and persistence rates were somewhat higher in middle age (44.5% at 43–52) than at 21–23 (32.4%), an age difference of borderline significance that disappeared with multiple imputation. Offset was common at every age. Becoming a parent went with lower odds, and getting a job with higher odds, of new onset in the reference group of women aged 21–37; the persistence findings rest on three-way interaction terms from sparse cells, one of which (new job) was not significant with multiple imputation.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract speaks of the 'effects' of life transitions varying across the lifespan and between men and women. The Results call becoming a parent 'a protective factor against persistence' for older men (OR 0.02) and report a new job lowering persistence in older men (OR 0.03); the Discussion calls the onset associations 'consistent across gender and age'. Gaps: (1) 0.02 and 0.03 are the three-way interaction terms of Table 3, not odds ratios for older men; under the table's reference coding the implied odds ratios for men aged 38+ are about 0.2 and 0.1 (editors' arithmetic from rounded values; no interval can be computed); (2) 'consistent across gender and age' is inferred from non-significant interactions with wide intervals, which do not show that the associations are the same; (3) 'protective' and 'effects' are causal words, while the Limitations say the results should not be taken to imply a causal effect, because transitions were measured over the same interval and people select into roles; (4) the abstract reports that persistence increased with age without saying that the result was marginal (p=.047) and absent with imputation and with a continuous-diagnosis definition; (5) offset is called only a minor contributor to the age gradient from shares and rates by age, without a formal decomposition of the prevalence difference. The descriptive headline, that falling onset and recurrence rather than a peak of offset in the twenties drive the age gradient, follows from the results, subject to the cohort confounding the authors set aside; the overstatements are confined to the life-transition analysis.

timeline.event: Chilcoat & Breslau: members of a health maintenance organization aged 21–30 followed for 3.5 years; onset of DSM-III-R alcohol abuse or dependence was higher in those stably single and persistence lower in those who married (as summarized in this paper's introduction). This paper found no association with change in marital status.

Grant, NLAES cross-sectional data: the youngest cohort had the highest past-year persistence among people with earlier dependence. This paper reproduced that result with Wave 1 NESARC data using Grant's retrospective definition (results not shown) and attributes the conflict with its own two-wave finding to the definition.
Crum et al., Baltimore Epidemiologic Catchment Area follow-up: incidence of DSM-III-R alcohol dependence over 12.6 years fell with age (as cited in this paper's discussion).

Dawson, Goldstein & Grant, NESARC Waves 1–2: 5.1% of people in full remission at Wave 1 had a recurrence by Wave 2, and age was negatively associated with recurrence (as cited in this paper's introduction).
Kalaydjian et al., NCS-R: remission from dependence was more frequent at younger ages (as cited), in the same direction as this paper's lower persistence at 21–23.
This study (online November 2011): decomposition of the age-prevalence curve of DSM-IV alcohol dependence in the two NESARC waves.

Related, same survey: Lopez-Quintero et al., NESARC Wave 1, probability of transition from first use to dependence on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine (a different question: cumulative transition from first use, not course after onset).

replication.where_it_stands: Within the paper, the decline of new onset with age agrees with earlier cross-sectional and longitudinal reports, while the age pattern of persistence depends on the definition: a retrospective definition reproduces Grant's (1997) falling persistence with age, the two-wave definition does not. No direct replication is named in the reading list for this round, and later NESARC analyses were not searched here. Claims may use the paper for the decomposition (new onset dominates the age gradient; offset is common at every age) and must present the life-transition results as associations from sparse subgroups.

funding.funder: NIH grants K05AA017242 and R01AA016392 to Kenneth J. Sher, and P60AA011998 to Andrew C. Heath (Acknowledgments). The survey itself is described as funded by the "National Institute of Alcoholism and Alcohol Abuse (NIAAA)" (so printed) and conducted by the US Census Bureau (Method › Participants).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the author manuscript on PMC.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of Missouri, Brown University and Washington University School of Medicine, most also with the Midwest Alcoholism Research Center. The Discussion's interpretation (age-related loss of vulnerability linked to personality maturation) draws on the senior author's own earlier analyses (Littlefield, Sher & Wood, 2009, 2010a, 2010b; Cicero, Epler & Sher, 2009), which this paper's data cannot test because the survey has no personality measures.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort-sequential study with yearly interviews of several birth cohorts from adolescence into old age, recording DSM symptoms, drinking, treatment and deaths (by record linkage) at every wave, would separate ageing from cohort, count onsets and recurrences without relying on lifetime recall, and show whether offset is lasting remission; for life transitions, within-person analyses that date each transition relative to the change in symptoms.

domains.note: The life-transition models adjust only for sex, race and age group; drinking level, other psychiatric and substance use disorders, education, income and family history are not adjusted, and people with alcohol dependence may be less likely to marry or become parents (selection into roles, acknowledged by the authors). The age gradient in transition rates is confounded with birth cohort and period, which the authors set aside.

Transitions are self-reported, coarse and coded from two time points: 'stable' merges married, single and divorced people (and employed and unemployed people), becoming a parent includes step, foster and adoptive parenthood, and changes of employment within the interval are missed (the authors expect this to underestimate employment effects). Age at Wave 2 is approximated as Wave 1 age plus three years.

A representative household sample, but the analysis includes only people alive and re-interviewed at Wave 2; the Wave 1 response rate is not reported in this paper; the at-risk groups depend on lifetime histories recalled at Wave 1.
Treatment for alcohol problems between the waves is neither reported nor adjusted, so offset may partly reflect treatment, and treatment could itself follow some transitions.

About 20% of Wave 1 respondents were not re-interviewed, with differences by sex, age, race and AD history; weights and multiple imputation gave similar results except that the persistence age effect and the new-job interaction lost significance; a further 10–15% of each at-risk group lacked transition data.

Self-reported AUDADIS-IV diagnoses. Persistence, offset and recurrence depend on a fixed 12-month window and the three-criterion threshold (the sensitivity analyses changed which age and interaction effects were significant), and new onset versus recurrence depends on recall of lifetime episodes at Wave 1, which the authors say may differ by age.

All Table 3 terms are printed and the sensitivity analyses are described, but 66 odds ratios were tested without correction, the text emphasises the significant three-way interactions, several analyses are 'not shown', and imputation results are given only where they differ.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For the associations of life transitions with the course of alcohol dependence the risk of bias is high: confounding is barely addressed, transitions and outcome were measured over the same interval, and the authors themselves rule out a causal reading. The descriptive decomposition (shares and rates of onset, persistence and recurrence by age) is not a causal estimate and is better protected by a representative sample, a standard interview and weighting for attrition; its main threats are cohort confounding of the age gradient, survivor-only follow-up, recall-based definitions of new onset and recurrence, and the 20% attrition. The paper may be cited for the descriptive picture (onset and recurrence fall steeply with age; offset is common at every age; about a third of cases persisted over three years in the early twenties and under half in middle age), always with the definition of offset, and not for effects of parenthood, employment or marriage.

key_findings.finding: NESARC Wave 1 (2001–2002) interviewed 43,093 US adults; 34,653 were re-interviewed at Wave 2 (2004–2005). Of the 1,433 with past-12-month DSM-IV alcohol dependence at Wave 2, 767 were new onsets (no lifetime AD at Wave 1), 422 persistent (past-12-month AD at Wave 1) and 244 recurrent (lifetime but not past-12-month AD at Wave 1).
key_findings.locator: Method › Participants; Method › Measures › Alcohol Dependence, 2nd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Among Wave 2 cases, the persistent share stayed about the same across age (29% at ages 21–23, 27% at 63+), the new-onset share fell (66% to 58%) and the recurrent share rose (5% to 15%).
key_findings.note: Only the youngest and oldest groups are given in the text; the values for the other age groups and the age-specific prevalences are printed only in Figure 1 (image, not extracted).

key_findings.finding: Among the people at risk, and adjusted for sex and race, the rates of new onset (Wald F=44.22, 6 df, p<.0001) and recurrence (Wald F=6.64, 6 df, p<.0001) fell significantly with age, while persistence rose (Wald F=2.28, 6 df, p=.047), a result not significant in the multiple-imputation analyses. The authors conclude that most of the age decline in prevalence comes from less onset and recurrence.

Persistence of dependence over the roughly three-year interval was 32.4% at ages 21–23 and 44.5% at ages 43–52, and the authors describe the persistence rate as relatively stable through the third decade while prevalence falls steeply.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Rethinking the Dramatic Age-Gradient in the Prevalence Curve of Alcohol Disorders, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Persistence here means meeting full DSM-IV criteria in the 12 months before each interview; the remainder (offset) includes people with one or two remaining symptoms and is not a remission definition. Treatment between the waves is not reported.

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from the unweighted counts in Table 2, all ages together: 422 of 1,172 people with past-12-month AD at Wave 1 (36%) met criteria again at Wave 2, so about 64% showed offset; 767 of 30,696 people without lifetime AD at Wave 1 (2.5%) had past-year AD at Wave 2 (new onset); 244 of 2,785 people with earlier AD (8.8%) had past-year AD again at Wave 2 (recurrence).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation, unweighted and not age-standardised; the paper does not print weighted totals for the three rates. The new-onset denominator includes people who had never drunk alcohol. New onset and recurrence count only dependence in the 12 months before Wave 2 (the authors call their approach 'time-sampling'): dependence that began or recurred and then remitted earlier in the roughly three-year interval is not counted, so 2.5% and 8.8% are past-year statuses at follow-up among the people at risk, not three-year cumulative incidences, and they understate onsets and recurrences over the interval.

key_findings.finding: With persistence redefined as AD at Wave 1 plus at least one dependence symptom at Wave 2, persistence rose in every age group with a similar age pattern, but the drop at 63+ made the age effect significant; with persistence redefined as continuous diagnosis across the interval, persistence showed no significant change with age. A stricter definition of recurrence gave a similar age pattern. The interaction results changed with the definition: under the at-least-one-symptom definition only the sex × age × new-job interaction was significant, and under the continuous-diagnosis definition only the parenthood interaction remained.
key_findings.locator: Results › Alternative Definitions of Persistence and Recurrence, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: No numbers are given for the sensitivity analyses.

key_findings.finding: New onset between the waves: becoming a parent went with lower odds (OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.18–0.83) and getting a new job with higher odds (OR 2.79, 1.19–6.55); men had higher odds than women (OR 1.87, 1.29–2.73) and people aged 38+ lower odds than those aged 21–37 (OR 0.22, 0.14–0.34). None of the interactions with age or sex was significant.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Onset column; Results › Role Transitions and Stability and Change of AD across Development, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Because interaction terms are in the model, these main effects are odds ratios in the reference groups (women aged 21–37, and for sex and age, people with no transitions), adjusted for race and the other terms. The sample is general-population; new onset was recorded prospectively across the waves, with the absence of earlier dependence taken from lifetime recall at Wave 1.

key_findings.finding: Persistence: becoming a parent went with lower odds of persistence in the reference group of women aged 21–37 (OR 0.22, 0.06–0.82), with significant sex × parenthood (4.56, 1.09–19.08), age × parenthood (9.56, 1.14–79.78) and sex × age × parenthood (0.02, 0.00–0.28) terms; the sex × age × new-job term was also significant (0.03, 0.00–0.48), but only the parenthood interaction remained significant with multiple imputation and with a continuous-diagnosis definition of persistence, while only the new-job interaction was significant with the at-least-one-symptom definition: neither survives every check. Sex was not associated with persistence (1.20, 0.67–2.15) or recurrence (1.00, 0.52–1.93), and no term was significant for recurrence.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Persistence and Recurrence columns; Results › Role Transitions and Stability and Change of AD across Development, 3rd paragraph; Results › Alternative Definitions of Persistence and Recurrence, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The text presents 0.02 and 0.03 as odds ratios for older men; they are interaction terms (see reporting issues). The intervals reflect sparse cells in a persistence model of 993 people at risk.

key_findings.finding: Change in marital status (becoming married or becoming separated, divorced or widowed) was not associated with new onset, persistence or recurrence in any model.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Discussion › Life Transitions and the Course of AD, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The authors suggest the merged 'stable' reference group (married, single or divorced at both waves) may have hidden an association; a whole-sample analysis showing the expected marriage pattern is 'not shown'.

key_findings.finding: Mean age at first drinking was 19.9 years in the new-onset group, 16.7 to 17.3 in the four groups with dependence at Wave 1 (persistent, recurrent, offset and non-recurrent), and 21.7 in the consistent non-diagnosis group; 65–72% of the five groups with past or present dependence were men against 44.7% of the consistent non-diagnosis group.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, rows Age First Drinking and % Male
key_findings.note: Descriptive only: age at first drinking was recalled and did not enter any model.

key_findings.finding: Retention at Wave 2 was about 80% and differed by sex, age, race and AD history (for example 85.6% with prior-to-past-year AD vs 81.2% with no diagnosis; 73.3% Asian and 73.4% Hispanic vs 83.6% White respondents); analyses with multiple imputation were reported as similar.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that because life transitions were measured over the same interval as the changes in dependence and people can select into roles, the results should not be read as causal effects of the transitions.

The authors report that Grant's retrospective definition of persistence (past-year dependence among people with dependence before the past year) reproduces a decline of persistence with age in the Wave 1 data, unlike their two-wave definition, and argue that the retrospective definition gives younger people less time to desist.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Rethinking the Dramatic Age-Gradient in the Prevalence Curve of Alcohol Disorders, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Results present 0.02 (0.00–0.28) as the odds ratio showing that becoming a parent protects older men against persistence, and 0.03 (0.00–0.48) as the odds ratio for a new job in older men. In Table 3 these are the sex × age × parenthood and sex × age × new-job interaction terms. Under the reference coding the table states (female, 21–37, not a parent, stable job), the implied odds ratios for men aged 38+ are the products of the main effect and the three relevant interaction terms: 0.22 × 4.56 × 9.56 × 0.02 ≈ 0.19 for parenthood and 0.84 × 2.14 × 1.90 × 0.03 ≈ 0.10 for a new job (editors' arithmetic; with the rounding of the printed terms, about 0.14 to 0.25 and 0.08 to 0.12).
reporting_issues.consequence: The implied associations are much weaker than the printed terms suggest: about ten times for parenthood (0.19 against 0.02) and about three times for a new job (0.10 against 0.03). Their intervals cannot be computed from the table, and the printed values must not be quoted as odds ratios for older men.

reporting_issues.issue: The onset main effects (parenthood 0.39; new job 2.79) are described as applying 'regardless of the age or sex' of participants, and in the Discussion as consistent across gender and age, but with interaction terms in the model they are the odds ratios for women aged 21–37; the absence of a significant interaction (for example age × parenthood 0.55, 0.11–2.86) does not show that the association is the same in other groups. Conversely, the significant persistence main effect of parenthood (0.22, 0.06–0.82, women aged 21–37) is not mentioned in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should state the onset associations for the reference group or as average associations with unknown heterogeneity, and should not describe the parenthood–persistence association as limited to older men.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions attribute most of the decrease in dependence over the life course to the reduction of onset and recurrence 'in addition to the increase in persistence', but a rise in persistence with age would raise prevalence, not lower it.
reporting_issues.consequence: A wording error in the Conclusions; the Results and Discussion make clear that falling onset and recurrence, not persistence, account for the decline. The sentence should not be paraphrased as written.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 (retention at Wave 2) is headed N=28,482, a number that matches neither the Wave 1 sample (43,093) nor the Wave 2 sample (34,653) and is not explained in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator of the retention percentages is unclear; the overall retention can be taken only as 'approximately 80%', which agrees with 34,653 of 43,093 (80.4%, editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the persistent group had a smaller proportion of married people 'at both waves' and the offset group fewer parents 'at both waves', but by the table's own subscripts the persistent group did not differ from the offset group in marriage at Wave 1 or from the onset and offset groups at Wave 2, and the offset group did not differ from the persistent and onset groups in parenthood at Wave 2.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Role Transitions and Stability and Change of AD across Development, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Descriptive overstatement of group differences; use the subscripted table, not the text, for these comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: The persistence result is described as an 'increasing trend with age', but the test reported is a 6-df Wald F test of any difference among seven age groups, not a trend test, and in one sensitivity analysis persistence fell at 63+.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 3rd paragraph; Results › Alternative Definitions of Persistence and Recurrence, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction and shape of the age pattern of persistence come from Figure 2 (an image) rather than from a test; together with its loss of significance under imputation and under the continuous definition, persistence should be described as roughly stable with age.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion cites Crum et al. (2005) as reporting that the incidence of DSM-III-R dependence over 12.6 years fell from 52.7% at ages 18–29 to 4.3% at 65 and over. A cumulative incidence above one half in a general-population cohort would be far above this paper's own onset figures (2.5% over three years, unweighted, all ages).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion › Rethinking the Dramatic Age-Gradient in the Prevalence Curve of Alcohol Disorders, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The unit of the cited figures (percentage or a rate per person-years) should be checked in the primary paper before they are reused; they do not affect this paper's own results.

reporting_issues.issue: The Method gives SUDAAN 'version 10' with a 2004 citation, while the reference list cites SUDAAN Version 9.0 (2004).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Method › Analysis; References (Research Triangle Institute, 2004)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; no effect on the results.
